title: Hubble Finds a City of Very Old Stars
summary:
Look closely at this sparkling crowd of stars. Some of them are almost as old as the universe itself, and they may hold clues about how our Milky Way formed.

The Hubble Space Telescope has taken a stunning picture of thousands of stars shining in blue, gold, and orange. The picture, shared by the European Space Agency on November 5, shows Messier 30, or M30. It is a tightly packed group of stars about 27,500 light-years from Earth in Capricornus.

M30 is a globular cluster: a ball-shaped group of tens of thousands to millions of stars, all held together by gravity. Some are thought to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. The universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old.

Globular clusters are like time capsules from space. Their old stars hold chemical clues from when they formed, helping scientists learn about the Milky Way's early days.

It moves through the Milky Way against the galaxy's spin, so it may have been pulled in from somewhere else billions of years ago.
why_it_matters: Looking at very old stars is like opening a time capsule, helping us learn how the galaxy we live in came to be.
